# Review of Last Class

## Monte Carlo Estimate and Error

$$\tilde\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i \quad\text{is unbiased,}\qquad \tilde\sigma_n = \frac{\sigma_Y}{\sqrt{n}} \quad\text{is its standard error.}$$


## Questions?

{{< include _poll-prompt.qmd >}}

# Confidence Intervals

## MC Confidence Intervals

To get estimates of the error, we need to understand the distribution of errors.

The **Central Limit Theorem** says that sums of random variables converge to a Gaussian distribution.

Applying to the mean (which is effectively a sum):

$$\left\|\tilde{\mu}_n - \mu\right\| \to \mathcal{N}\left(0, \frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n}\right)$$


## Confidence Intervals

We can use this large-$n$ Gaussian approximation to get an $\alpha$-confidence interval.

$$\tilde\mu_n \pm \Phi^{-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sqrt{n}}$$

For 95%: $$\tilde\mu_n \pm 1.96\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sqrt{n}}.$$

## Reading a CI Correctly

**A 95% CI is not** "there is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval." According to the **frequentist** interpretation of statistics, the true value is fixed.

For any given experiment, the "true value" is either in or out of the constructed interval.

**The idea**: if you repeated this whole experiment many times, about 95% of the intervals you'd construct would contain the true value.

## Example: 95% CIs for N(0.4, 2)

```{julia}
#| label: fig-cis
#| code-fold: true
#| code-overflow: wrap
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap: "Display of 95% confidence intervals"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|  - "Sample Size 100"
#|  - "Sample Size 1,000"

# set up distribution
mean_true = 0.4
n_cis = 100 # number of CIs to compute
dist = Normal(mean_true, 2)

# use sample size of 100
samples = rand(dist, (100, n_cis))
# mapslices broadcasts over a matrix dimension, could also use a loop
sample_means = mapslices(mean, samples; dims=1)
sample_sd = mapslices(std, samples; dims=1) 
mc_sd = 1.96 * sample_sd / sqrt(100)
mc_ci = zeros(n_cis, 2) # preallocate
for i = 1:n_cis
    mc_ci[i, 1] = sample_means[i] - mc_sd[i]
    mc_ci[i, 2] = sample_means[i] + mc_sd[i]
end
# find which CIs contain the true value
ci_true = (mc_ci[:, 1] .< mean_true) .&& (mc_ci[:, 2] .> mean_true)
# compute percentage of CIs which contain the true value
ci_frac1 = 100 * sum(ci_true) ./ n_cis

# plot CIs
p1 = plot([mc_ci[1, :]], [1, 1], linewidth=3, color=:deepskyblue, label="95% Confidence Interval", title="Sample Size 100", yticks=:false, legend=:false)
for i = 2:n_cis
    if ci_true[i]
        plot!(p1, [mc_ci[i, :]], [i, i], linewidth=2, color=:deepskyblue, label=:false)
    else
        plot!(p1, [mc_ci[i, :]], [i, i], linewidth=2, color=:red, label=:false)
    end
end
vline!(p1, [mean_true], color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash, label="True Value") # plot true value as a vertical line
xaxis!(p1, "Estimate")
plot!(p1, size=(500, 350)) # resize to fit slide

# use sample size of 1000
samples = rand(dist, (1000, n_cis))
# mapslices broadcasts over a matrix dimension, could also use a loop
sample_means = mapslices(mean, samples; dims=1)
sample_sd = mapslices(std, samples; dims=1) 
mc_sd = 1.96 * sample_sd / sqrt(1000)
mc_ci = zeros(n_cis, 2) # preallocate
for i = 1:n_cis
    mc_ci[i, 1] = sample_means[i] - mc_sd[i]
    mc_ci[i, 2] = sample_means[i] + mc_sd[i]
end
# find which CIs contain the true value
ci_true = (mc_ci[:, 1] .< mean_true) .&& (mc_ci[:, 2] .> mean_true)
# compute percentage of CIs which contain the true value
ci_frac2 = 100 * sum(ci_true) ./ n_cis

# plot CIs
p2 = plot([mc_ci[1, :]], [1, 1], linewidth=3, color=:deepskyblue, label="95% Confidence Interval", title="Sample Size 1,000", yticks=:false, legend=:false)
for i = 2:n_cis
    if ci_true[i]
        plot!(p2, [mc_ci[i, :]], [i, i], linewidth=2, color=:deepskyblue, label=:false)
    else
        plot!(p2, [mc_ci[i, :]], [i, i], linewidth=2, color=:red, label=:false)
    end
end
vline!(p2, [mean_true], color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash, label="True Value") # plot true value as a vertical line
xaxis!(p2, "Estimate")
plot!(p2, size=(500, 350)) # resize to fit slide

display(p1)
display(p2)
```

`{julia} Int64(round(ci_frac1))`% of the CIs contain the true value (left) vs. `{julia} Int64(round(ci_frac2))`% (right)


## MC Example: Dice

What is the probability of rolling 4 dice for a total of 19?

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|14-17|18-20|22-25"

function dice_roll_repeated(n_trials, n_dice)
    dice_dist = DiscreteUniform(1, 6) 
	roll_results = zeros(n_trials)
	for i=1:n_trials
		roll_results[i] = sum(rand(dice_dist, n_dice))
	end
	return roll_results
end

nsamp = 10_000
# roll four dice 10,000 times
rolls = dice_roll_repeated(nsamp, 4) 

# initialize storage for frequencies by sample length
avg_freq = zeros(length(rolls)) 
# initialize storage for standard error of estimate
std_freq = zeros(length(rolls))
# compute average frequencies of 19
avg_freq[1] = (rolls[1] == 19)
std_freq[1] = 0 # no standard error for the first sample

for i in 2:length(rolls)
    avg_freq[i] = (avg_freq[i-1] * (i-1) + (rolls[i] == 19)) / i
    std_freq[i] = std(rolls[1:i] .== 19) / sqrt(i)
end
```
:::

## MC Example: Dice

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

plt = plot(
    avg_freq, ribbon=1.96 * std_freq,
    xlim = (1, nsamp),
    ylim = (0, 0.1),
    legend = :false,
    xlabel="Iteration",
    ylabel="Estimate",
    left_margin=10mm,
    bottom_margin=10mm,
    right_margin=10mm,
    color=:black,
    linewidth=3
)
plot!(size=(1200, 500))

hline!(plt, [0.0432], color="red", 
    linestyle=:dash) 

```

## MC Example: Dice

After 10,000 iterations, the 95% confidence interval for the MC estimate is `{julia} round(100 * avg_freq[end]; digits=1)` $\pm$ `{julia} round(196 * std_freq[end]; digits=1)`%.

**Is this good enough? Should we keep going?**

# Back to the DO

## Framing the DO Question for Monte Carlo

**What is the probability that the minimum DO falls below the 2.5 mg/L standard on a randomly chosen day?**

Recall Streeter-Phelps. Today, three of its inputs vary from day to day, not just the CBOD load.

## Sampling the Three Inputs

| Input | Distribution (mg/L) |
|:--|:--|
| Incoming DO, $C_0$ | $\mathcal{N}(6.2, 0.5^2)$, at most 7 |
| CBOD, $B_0$ | $\mathcal{N}(9, 1.5^2)$, at least 0 |
| NBOD, $N_0$ | $\mathcal{N}(7, 1^2)$, at least 0 |

We draw them independently. CBOD and NBOD come from the same effluent: is that reasonable?

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: false

do_params = let
    ka, kc, kn = 0.6, 0.4, 0.25   # reaeration, CBOD decay, NBOD decay [1/d]
    Cs, U = 7, 5                  # saturation DO [mg/L], velocity [km/d]
    L = 40                        # reach length [km]
    standard = 2.5                # DO standard [mg/L]
    (; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, L, standard)
end

# The three uncertain inputs [mg/L]; truncation keeps every draw physical
incoming_DO = truncated(Normal(6.2, 0.5); upper=7)
incoming_CBOD = truncated(Normal(9, 1.5); lower=0)
incoming_NBOD = truncated(Normal(7, 1); lower=0)

function do_min(C0, B0, N0, params; dx=0.1)
    steps = Int(round(params.L / dx))
    C = C0
    lowest = C
    for i in 1:steps
        x = (i - 1) * dx
        C = C + dx * ((params.ka * (params.Cs - C) - params.kc * B0 * exp(-params.kc * x / params.U)
                        - params.kn * N0 * exp(-params.kn * x / params.U)) / params.U)
        lowest = min(lowest, C)
    end
    return lowest
end

# One Monte Carlo sample: draw all three inputs, then check the standard
function violates(params; dx=0.1)
    C0 = rand(incoming_DO)
    B0 = rand(incoming_CBOD)
    N0 = rand(incoming_NBOD)
    return do_min(C0, B0, N0, params; dx=dx) < params.standard
end
```

## Watching the Estimate Settle

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mc-do
#| fig-cap: "Running Monte Carlo estimate of P(violation), with its 95% confidence band."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

Random.seed!(4750)
N = 20_000
draws = [violates(do_params) for _ in 1:N]
running_p = cumsum(draws) ./ (1:N)
running_se = zeros(N)
running_se[1] = NaN
for i in 2:N
    running_se[i] = sqrt(running_p[i] * (1 - running_p[i]) / i)
end

p_mc = plot(1:N, running_p, ribbon=1.96 .* running_se, xscale=:log10,
    color=:black, linewidth=3, fillalpha=0.25, fillcolor=cb_blue,
    xlabel="Number of samples  n", ylabel="P(violation)", legend=false,
    ylims=(0, 1))
hline!(p_mc, [running_p[end]], color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2)
plot!(p_mc, size=(1100, 460), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)
```

## The Number, With Honesty About Its Uncertainty

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("| \$n\$ | estimate | 95% CI |")
println("|---:|---:|:---|")
for n in [5, 20, 100, 500, 2000, 20_000]
    p = running_p[n]
    lo, hi = round(p - 1.96 * running_se[n], digits=2), round(p + 1.96 * running_se[n], digits=2)
    println("| \$$(n)\$ | \$$(round(p, digits=2))\$ | \$[$(lo), $(hi)]\$ |")
end
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
five_low = round(running_p[5] - 1.96 * running_se[5], digits=2)
five_high = round(running_p[5] + 1.96 * running_se[5], digits=2)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**At $n=5$ the interval runs from `{julia} five_low` to `{julia} five_high`** --- nearly the whole unit range, with a lower end below zero. Five runs, like the ensemble that posed this question in the Streeter-Phelps lecture, are not enough to trust.
:::

# Justifying a Sample Size

## The Rubric You Will Be Graded On

::: {.quote}
> +2 for justification of Monte Carlo sample size. **Deadly Sin: No points will be given for a Monte Carlo solution with an arbitrary sample size.** +2 for an estimate of the Monte Carlo standard error. +1 for setting a seed for reproducibility.

::: {.cite}
--- the Monte Carlo Rubric, `policies/rubric.qmd`
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
This is the **same discipline as $\Delta t$ in Week 4**, with $n$ in place of the step size:
:::

## The Same Discipline, a Different Knob

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
**Simulation** (Week 4)

- pick $\Delta t$ from a characteristic timescale
- halve it; see if the answer moves
- error $\sim \Delta t$
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
**Monte Carlo** (today)

- pick $n$ from a target CI half-width
- double it; see if the estimate moves
- error $\sim 1/\sqrt{n}$
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Both times: name a quantity of interest, refine the knob, estimate what's left, **report what you did**. Both rubrics penalize not doing it.
:::

## The Sentence You Copy Into Your Homework

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

p2, se2 = round(running_p[2000], digits=3), round(running_se[2000], digits=4)
p4 = round(running_p[4000], digits=3)
half_width2 = 1.96 * se2
lo, hi = round(p2 - half_width2, digits=2), round(p2 + half_width2, digits=2)
change = round(abs(p4 - p2), digits=4)
# The wording follows the numbers, so the sentence stays true for any seed.
if change < se2
    comparison = "less than one standard error"
    verdict = "so \$n=2{,}000\$ is sufficient for this analysis."
elseif change < half_width2
    comparison = "less than the 95% half-width"
    verdict = "so \$n=2{,}000\$ is sufficient for this analysis."
else
    comparison = "more than the 95% half-width"
    verdict = "so \$n=2{,}000\$ is not yet enough."
end
println("> \"I estimated \$P(\\text{DO} < 2.5\\ \\text{mg/L})\$ with \$n = 2{,}000\$ Monte Carlo ",
        "samples, seeded for reproducibility. The estimate is \$$(p2)\$ with a Monte Carlo ",
        "standard error of \$$(se2)\$, giving a 95% CI of \$[$(lo), $(hi)]\$. Doubling to ",
        "\$n=4{,}000\$ changed the estimate by \$$(change)\$, $(comparison), ", verdict, "\"")
```

# Two Errors, One Answer

## You Now Have Two Knobs

Every number you report from this model is shaped by two choices you made:

::: {.incremental}
- $\Delta x$, the spatial step --- Week 4's knob.
- $n$, the number of samples --- today's.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Refining either one costs time. **Which should you refine?**
:::

## Put Them in the Same Units

The two errors are not comparable until they describe the same quantity. So express both as an error in **the violation probability**, which is the number you would actually report.

- **Grid error**: hold $n$ and the seed fixed, vary $\Delta x$, see how $P$ moves.
- **Sampling error**: hold $\Delta x$ fixed, and read the half-width $1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

## Measuring the Grid Error

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

function violation_fraction(grid_step, sample_count, seed)
    Random.seed!(seed)
    violations = 0
    for _ in 1:sample_count
        if violates(do_params; dx=grid_step)
            violations += 1
        end
    end
    return violations / sample_count
end

grid_steps = [1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1]
reference_p = violation_fraction(0.02, 3000, 99)

grid_estimates = zeros(length(grid_steps))
for i in 1:length(grid_steps)
    grid_estimates[i] = violation_fraction(grid_steps[i], 3000, 99)
end
grid_errors = abs.(grid_estimates .- reference_p)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("| \$\\Delta x\$ (km) | \$P\$ | error vs. fine grid |")
println("|---:|---:|---:|")
for i in 1:length(grid_steps)
    println("| \$$(grid_steps[i])\$ | \$$(round(grid_estimates[i], digits=3))\$ | \$$(round(grid_errors[i], digits=3))\$ |")
end
```

## Measuring the Sampling Error

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("| \$n\$ | 95% half-width |")
println("|---:|---:|")
for n_samples in [100, 500, 2000, 8000]
    half_width = 1.96 * sqrt(reference_p * (1 - reference_p) / n_samples)
    println("| \$$(n_samples)\$ | \$$(round(half_width, digits=3))\$ |")
end
```

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Sampling error falls as $1/\sqrt{n}$ --- predictably, and as slowly as we warned on Wednesday.
:::

## Two Errors, Two Rates

```{julia}
#| label: fig-two-rates
#| fig-cap: "Left: measured grid error against step size, with a slope-1 reference. Right: the reported 95% half-width against sample count, with a slope -1/2 reference. Both on log-log axes."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

# Sampling error measured against this chain's own long-run estimate.
# The sampling error we plot is the half-width we would actually report, not
# one chain's realised error -- a single chain's error is itself random and
# does not fall smoothly.
sample_sizes = [50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10_000]
sampling_errors = zeros(length(sample_sizes))
for i in 1:length(sample_sizes)
    sampling_errors[i] = 1.96 * sqrt(reference_p * (1 - reference_p) / sample_sizes[i])
end

p_grid = plot(grid_steps, grid_errors, xscale=:log10, yscale=:log10,
    markershape=:circle, markersize=7, color=cb_vermillion, linewidth=3,
    xlabel="Δx  [km]", ylabel="error in P", label="measured", legend=:bottomright,
    xticks=(grid_steps, string.(grid_steps)))
plot!(p_grid, grid_steps, grid_errors[1] .* (grid_steps ./ grid_steps[1]),
    color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash, label="slope 1")

p_samp = plot(sample_sizes, sampling_errors, xscale=:log10, yscale=:log10,
    markershape=:circle, markersize=7, color=cb_blue, linewidth=3,
    xlabel="n", ylabel="95% half-width in P", label="reported", legend=:bottomleft)
plot!(p_samp, sample_sizes, sampling_errors[1] .* sqrt.(sample_sizes[1] ./ sample_sizes),
    color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash, label="slope -1/2")

plot(p_grid, p_samp, layout=(1, 2), size=(1100, 430), left_margin=12mm,
    right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)
```

## One You Measure, One You Predict

Note what had to be done to get each panel.

::: {.incremental}
- **Grid error**: there is no formula. You found it by *refining and comparing* --- the same thing Week 4 made you do.
- **Sampling error**: you can write it down **before running anything**, from $1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
That asymmetry is why the grid error is the one people skip. Nothing prompts you to look for it, and no formula hands it to you.
:::

## Which One Dominates?

```{julia}
#| output: false
coarse_grid_error = grid_errors[1]
typical_half_width = 1.96 * sqrt(reference_p * (1 - reference_p) / 2000)
error_ratio = coarse_grid_error / typical_half_width
```

At $\Delta x = 1$ km and $n = 2{,}000$ --- both perfectly reasonable-looking choices --- the grid error is **`{julia} round(error_ratio, digits=1)` times** the sampling half-width.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Refining $n$ here buys you almost nothing. The answer is limited by the grid, not the samples.
:::

## The Error You Can See

Your confidence interval is computed from $n$ alone. **It knows nothing about $\Delta x$.**

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
So a report that says $P =$ `{julia} round(running_p[2000], digits=2)` $\pm$ `{julia} round(1.96 * running_se[2000], digits=2)` is quoting a precise answer to a model that has not been resolved. The interval is honest about the error it measures and silent about the one that dominates.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Report both, or the interval misleads.**
:::

# From Probability to Risk

## You Have a Number. Is It Risk?

We estimated the probability that dissolved oxygen falls below the standard on a given day.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
That is a real and useful number. It is also **not** a risk estimate.
:::

## What Risk Means

The [*Society for Risk Analysis* definition](https://www.sra.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/SRA-Glossary-FINAL.pdf):

::: {.quote}
> "risk" involves uncertainty about the effects/implications of an activity with respect to something that humans value (such as health, well-being, wealth, property or the environment), often focusing on negative, undesirable consequences.
:::

## Risk Is Not Probability

**"Risk" is not just another word for probability.** It involves:

::: {.incremental}
- uncertainty;
- *undesirable* outcomes;
- **effects**, not just the events themselves.
:::

## Components of Risk

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
Several things combine to produce risk:

- Probability of a **hazard**;
- **Exposure** to that hazard;
- **Vulnerability** to the outcomes;
- Socioeconomic **responses**.
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
![Overview of the Components of Risk](figures/simpson_risk.svg)

::: {.caption}
Source: [Simpson et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oneear.2021.03.005)
:::
:::
::::

## Our Model Contains One of Four

$P(\text{DO} < 2.5)$ is a **hazard** statistic, and nothing more.

::: {.incremental}
- Who is **exposed**? Which reach, whose water intake, which fishery?
- How **vulnerable** are they? A brief dip matters differently to a trout stream than to an industrial intake.
- What is the **response**? A warning system, a permit change, a treatment upgrade.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
None of those three are in the model. **Managing risk needs all four, and simulation gives you one.**
:::

# Practical Notes

## Pseudorandomness and Seeds

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=40%}
Random number generators are not *really* random --- only **pseudorandom**, and deterministic given a seed.

**Always set a seed.** It's how your results (and your grader's) reproduce.
:::
::: {.column width=60%}
![XKCD 221: Random Number](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/random_number.png){width=90%}

::: {.caption}
Source: [XKCD #221](https://xkcd.com/221/)
:::
:::
::::

# Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule

## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- A confidence interval describes the **procedure**, not the one interval you happened to construct.
- **Sample size needs justification**, exactly like Week 4's step size: pick $n$ from a target precision, double it and check, report the standard error.
- Five samples were nowhere near enough to trust the DO ensemble --- now you know how to say precisely how far short they fell.
- **Two errors sit in every answer**, and they fall at different rates. Refining the wrong knob buys nothing.
- **Your confidence interval measures one of them and is silent about the other.**
- A violation probability is a **hazard** statistic. Risk needs exposure, vulnerability, and response as well --- and none of those is in the model.
:::
